title: Ad Armenium Epistola 'De Ratione Fidei'
author: Agnellus Ravennas Episcopus

passages.original: Ad haec exigendum est ut dicat: Quando voluit generare Filium, habueritne virtutem generandi, et sapientiam hoc ipsum volendi? Si dixerit : N< n habebat, confutas blasphemum : Si dixerit: Ilabebat, obtines victoriam : Filius enim, ut dicit Apostolus, Dei Patris virtus est et sapientia (I Cor. I, 24). Nam qui dicit: Virtutem non habuit, blasphemat : qui dicit: Sapientiam 1.0.1 habuit, blasphemat. Hoc quare? quia in capite libri sui Arius dicit : Fuit Deus, quando Pater non fuit : ut videatur inir .ducere minorem Filium ad honorem Palris. Dlasphemat igitur Patrem multis modis : primo jam, quia non potest stare ut dicatur : Qui cat misit me, quia jam non potest dici: Qui esi, qui heri alius fuit, et hodie alins est.
passages.english: In answer to this he must be required to say: when he willed to beget the Son, did he have the power of begetting, and the wisdom to will this very thing? If he says, "He did not have [it]," you refute the blasphemer. If he says, "He had [it]," you win the victory, for the Son, as the Apostle says, is the power and wisdom of God the Father (1 Cor. 1:24). For whoever says, "He did not have power," blasphemes; whoever says, "He did not have wisdom," blasphemes. Why is this? Because at the head of his book Arius says: "There was [a time when there was] God, when there was no Father," so that he may be seen to bring in the Son as lesser, to the honour of the Father. He therefore blasphemes the Father in many ways: first, because it cannot then stand that it be said, "He who is sent me," since it can no longer be said, "He who is," of one who yesterday was one thing and today is another.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "N< n" = Non; "Ilabebat" = Habebat; "1.0.1 habuit" read as "non habuit"; "inir .ducere" = introducere; "Palris" = Patris; "Dlasphemat" = Blasphemat; "Qui cat" and "Qui esi" = Qui est (cf. Exod. 3:14); "alins" = alius. The Arian slogan "Fuit Deus, quando Pater non fuit" is rendered literally with a bracketed supplement; the sense is that God existed before he was Father. "ad honorem Patris" could also mean "in relation to the Father's honour", i.e. as inferior in honour.
